#1500. Outstanding Leeds cut short Jaissle’s Newcastle honeymoon

The noise started in a corner of the South Stand, early in the second half. It was muffled at first, but as the ball popped from one white shirt to another, it became louder and louder, sweeping around the stadium: here was the soundtrack for a humiliation.

“Olé! Olé! Olé!” they roared and why not? Leeds were ripping Newcastle to pieces, knocking passes around them as if they were training-ground mannequins. Football has become a sport that leaves people increasingly vexed, but this was a night when – for the locals, at least – it was almost a throwback.

There was energy and ferocious tackling, a No 9 soaring like centre-forwards used to in the not-too-distant past and lots of goals as Leeds cut loose and abruptly ended whatever honeymoon Matthias Jaissle had been experiencing in charge of Newcastle.

“I suppose in football you can always find something to moan about,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “But this was a top-class performance.”

It has felt suspiciously like Newcastle’s start has been like an overstuffed plastic shopping bag, the handles straining to the point of snapping. Eventually they fell asunder. Leeds ran all over them and were too smart, slick and hungry, not to mention ruthless. No wonder Jaissle had nowhere to go.

The home fans were adamant this was one of the best nights Leeds have experienced under Farke and if they were prepared to say as much, you had an obligation to listen. Forget how wretched Newcastle were, Leeds had produced a performance to enable imaginations to run wild.

Centre to it all was Ao Tanaka, with his desire to keep Leeds playing forward, but it felt wrong to talk about one man when you had the unstoppable Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who would be substituted to a standing ovation, and the ubiquitous James Justin, among others.

"He just cannot stop scoring at Elland Road" 🔥Dominic Calvert-Lewin makes it 2-0 to Leeds! pic.twitter.com/Pv1TEpc5Qj

The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.

Ao Tanaka's deflected effort puts Leeds ahead! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/cYXVi3LOAO

Leeds were running even quicker by this point, pressing as if their lives depended on it and making tackles that were lustily acclaimed in the stands. Steur completely short-circuited in the bedlam and a ridiculous pass on the edge of his area was pounced upon by Bogle.

Out went a ball to Justin, whose cross was whipped into the penalty area, where Calvert-Lewin had climbed to get his head to it, though replays indicated his effort glanced off Bogle’s head – determining the true scorer will make for an interesting conversation.

Calvert-Lewin, at least, got the reward his efforts deserved on the cusp of half-time, spinning away from Miley and chopping inside Sven Botman before delivering the kind of finish that should make Thomas Tuchel take note when selecting his next England squad this week.

"They are relentless!"Dominic Calvert-Lewin caps off a dominant first-half from Leeds 💪 pic.twitter.com/S6kQykOMW9

The gloss, after those “olés”, was applied in the 59th minute when Noah Okafor put a realistic hue on the score, ramming in a finish in front of the Kop and leaving Newcastle open to the crudest mocking for the amount of money they have spent to resemble such a disorganised rabble.

A wonderful strike with equally brilliant celebrations from Noah Okafor! 🕺 pic.twitter.com/Ce1ueKtH4x

Bazoumana Touré, at least, scored a consolation goal, but Jaissle barely flickered as it went in and the emotion belonged to Farke, who thundered on to the pitch at the final whistle and sought out his captain, Ampadu, who had erred in allowing Newcastle’s substitute to profit.

“That was an unnecessary goal to concede and I so wanted us to keep a clean sheet,” Farke sighed. “We deserved a clean sheet and I couldn’t help myself. I had to tell him because I am sometimes a perfectionist. We must try to stay humble, but we can be an outstanding team.”

And this, for certain, was an outstanding night.

[It was brutal out there?] That’s football. That’s the Premier League. It was clear from the start and I have said it many times. We will have ups and downs and challenges all the way. Tonight we faced that challenge. It’s tough and difficult to digest. But there is a chance to learn out of that and there’s a long time until our next match at home and that is good.

It’s clear with our young squad that there will be ups and downs and you have to bring the fundamentals on the pitch against such a physical team. Leeds are so intense, we couldn’t match that physicality. There are other aspects of course but I don’t want to make excuses. We want to learn out of it and be better.

[Were you overwhelmed as a team?] No. If you don’t bring that physicality on the pitch, you struggle.

Exactly this [message to the players]. Bring your fundamentals and we build on it. [Can you bounce back from this in your next game?] Of course. [Is your confidence hit?] No

For each manager it would be a nightmare after such a game to concede so late and not have the well-deserved clean sheet. Of course I was not happy about the situation. Doesn’t take anything away from my boys who were magnificent. Terrific start with eight points but there’s never a perfect performance. There’s always something to moan about. At very rare points [in the season] I have to criticise [for conceding].

Energy, quality, good structure, in an out of possession, which is complicated against Newcastle, In pressing them you always have to be aware of their unbelievable pace and strength in counter-attacks. We found this balance today and in the first half particularly we were dominant.

We have a good fitness level now. Need to find the right triggers to press. It’s a lot of well-structured work on the training ground. We had more chances to score tonight but overall I am very happy with our performance.

[Calvert-Lewin being praised] It is well deserved. He is in outstanding shape and plays with lots of confidence. I expect him to lead the group with some other players. His work-rate is never in doubt and to me he is one of the best strikers in the league.

The ref told me at half-time that they’ve taken it off me. I didn’t know he [Bogle] was there to be fair. I just got up and went ‘Bang!’ It is what it is. I’ll take the assist!

I didn’t know anything about it [being given credit for the second goal]. I said to the ref, I don’t fancy telling him [Calvert-Lewin]. To be fair he’s still raging. He’s raging with the goal but happy with the result.

It’s about having an understanding with the players around you. With Dom up there, you know he’s going to win everything so you have to get the runners around him.

It’s about the rotation like today. When James Justin goes wider there’s space inside. Dom occupies two centre-backs so there’s always pockets.

Regardless of the scoreline it was a tough game physically. They’re a very good side. We take it game by game, not to get carried away. Everyone’s ambitious in their own way but we have to take it game by game.

A proper stuffing for Newcastle as Leeds continue to impress and climb up to third.

James pounces on a loose ball, dribbles infield from the right. No one bothers to close him down so he eventually has a shot, blazing over with his left from 20 yards.

Late free-kick for Leeds after Livramento bundled Aaronson over. Wilson chips from the left to the far post and Muharemovic heads it back acros goal looking for a team-mate but none had made the run.

Leeds 4 Newcastle 1 (Touré) No clean sheet for Leeds. Farke is fuming after the substitute exploits an error and scores with a left-foot shot that deflects off Justin.

Livramento drives the ball 60 yards looking for Barnes but the ball skids off the turf and into Trafford’s arms.

Crunching Bard tackle on Bamba sends the ball to James who lets fly from 22 yards into the shins of a Newcastle defender.

Bard is penalised for a trip on Barnes as the game peters out.

Ampadu and Bamba collide when fighting for a loose ball but there was nothing malicious in it.

Wissa escapes a booking for a snide kick at Muharemovic’s shin.

A debatable offside call which should have been left for VAR lets Trafford off the hook when he comes out of his area to clear a ball clipped over the top. He slices it to Toure and the ref stops the game but I think Bard was playing Wissa, who found Toure, onside.

Newcastle corner on the left headed out by Elvedi and Barnes recovers the ball to start another attack with the 18-yard line stacked with players. When the diagonal comes back from left to right Barnes heads it behind for a goalkick.

Willock hooks a half-volley on to the roof of the net.

Bard → GudmundssonAaronson → OkaforWilson → Tanaka

Newcastle free-kick for a trip on Willock. Hall takes and Leeds head it out for a throw-in.

Livramento improves the quality of crosses with two that at least find the middle of the box even if they were headed away by Elvedi and Justin respectively.

Newcastle are enjoying more possession but the crossing has been awful when they do get down the flanks, Touré the latest offender.

Barnes shoots down Trafford’s throat. Barnes had thrown himself down in the box moments earlier and there was a VAR check but there was nothing like the contact required to send him swan-diving on to the grass.

Wissa gets down the right and whips over a low cross but Willock’s touch was too heavy.

There was a piece in the Athletic today saying Newcastle pivoted to Hornicek instead of pursuing Trafford again because he had a very high ceiling and was younger. He hasn’t caught much here, dropping the ball even when he chooses not to punch.

Matthias Jaissle promised high intensity, high octane, front foot football when he was interviewed for the Newcastle job. He and sporting director Ross Wilson have repeated that promise several times since he was appointed. There has been no sign of it since the opening weekend against Liverpool.

Newcastle are passive, they look disorganised in midfield and weak at the back. Oh and they barely apply pressure let alone attack dangerously.

These are early days but this performance and result had been coming. A pretty brutal reality check after all the positive noise and bold predictions in pre-season. This defeat will drop Newcastle to 12th in the table, where they finished last season under Eddie Howe.

Leeds 4 Newcastle 0 (Okafor) Ampadu hurls it into the box. A defender heads it to the edge of the area where Okafor thumps a left-footed half-volley in off the right post.

A wonderful strike with equally brilliant celebrations from Noah Okafor! 🕺 pic.twitter.com/Ce1ueKtH4x

Livramento slides in to stop Okafor’s drive down the left, giving Leeds another opportunity to throw it long.

Triple change: Livramento → DedicTouré → Fernandez-PardoWillock → Murphy

Leeds catch Newcastle playing short from the back. Stach blindsides Steur 20 yards out, tackles him, cuts inside then bends a left foot shot into the side-netting.

After Hall stings Trafford’s palms with a strike from distance. Newcastle want a penalty when the ball hits Tanaka’s arm … but it was outside the area and then Murphy, in frustration, chops down Gudmundsson and takes the booking as an occupational hazard.

Elvedi sloppily gives the ball way to Wissa who tries to set Fernandez-Pardo through down the left. Justin sticks with him and Bogle mops up after Justin was tripped.

Gudmundsson does the upended beetle when he tries to break from the corner and collides with a Newcastle player. He claims he was fouled and wthrashes about like a RL player after he’s tackled. He continues to do a Rumpelstiltskin polka of peevishness towards the ref for a while.

Newcastle corner on the left that Trafford backpedals to tip behind for another.

No changes at half-time for Newcastle as they kick off. Leeds break through the middle quickly and Calvert-Lewin seems to push the ball past Botman and shapes to shoot before Steur slides in with a crucial tackle just inside the box.

The first goal is now an own goal. The explanation is that Tanaka’s shot was on target but the deflection from Steur meant it was going wide until it hit Miley.

Now the second goal has been credited to Bogle as Calvert-Lewin’s header struck the top of his head before it went in.

You could not say that this scoreline is undeserved. Newcastle are being demolished physically. The central midfield two – Steur and Miley – just don’t have the power to screen their defence.

Leeds 3 Newcastle 0 (Calvert-Lewin) Leeds are running all over Newcastle who seem physically flimsy. Calvert-Lewin chops in from the left on to a flick-on, the ball takes a deflection off the Newcastle captain and he steers it into the far corner with a right-foot shot.

"They are relentless!"Dominic Calvert-Lewin caps off a dominant first-half from Leeds 💪 pic.twitter.com/S6kQykOMW9

Calvert-Lewin is booked for catching Botman in the face with a straight arm rather than a swinging arm. ‘Reckless but not violent.’ Trafford had punchd the corner away at the back post to set Leeds off on a counter.

Tanaka gives the ball away carelessly in midfield and Newcastle work it to Wissa who chops inside past Elvedi, hangs out his own leg looking for contact and hits the deck. The ref waves play on and the ball runs to Barnes in the left of the area. He shapes to shoot but Muharemovic sprinted over to make a fine block-tackle, forcing it behind for a corner.

Newcastle are rocking here. They cannot win a tackle.

For those of us who have watched all Newcastle United’s games this season, this was coming. They do not have any consistent attacking threat, they do no create chances and they are not secure at the back either.

They’ve survived by converting the very few chances they create in games but they have not even had a shot in the first half here.

Leeds should be three up after Hornicek fumbled Gudmundsson’s shot from the left. The ball falls to Calvert-Lewin five yards out and he triesto dink it over the keeper who recovers well to smother it.

Leeds 2 Newcastle 0 (Calvert-Lewin) Newcastle try to play the ball out from the back, give it away cheaply to Bogle who feeds Justin haring down the right. He is ostensibly the right centre-back but he is a full-back by trade and stands up a perfect near-post cross that Calvert-Lewin hangs in the air to bury with the firmest of headers. In fact it transpires that his downward header struck Bogle and another deflection benefits rampant Leeds –162 seconds between the goals.

"He just cannot stop scoring at Elland Road" 🔥Dominic Calvert-Lewin makes it 2-0 to Leeds! pic.twitter.com/Pv1TEpc5Qj

Leeds 1 Newcastle 0 (Tanaka) Good move, spawny finish. Tanaka sprays a pass out to Okafor who drives at Dedic then picks out Tanaka who had held his run. He cushions the pass then lets fly. The ball hits Steur, deflects on to Miley and then loops into the right of the goal with Hornicek understandably stranded.

Ao Tanaka's deflected effort puts Leeds ahead! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/cYXVi3LOAO

Good tackle by Steur on Bogle stops the Leeds right-back flying forward after Calvert-Lewin’s flick-on.

Newcastle really are not afraid to launch the ball forward are they? Football tactics are constantly evolving and fashions come back around. What better way to play through a press than to bypass the midfield completely? The hope is it will also cause the centre-backs problems, get them facing their own goal under pressure from one of Newcastle’s rapid forward players in a foot race.

It almost worked a couple of times in the first half but it should be pointed out that the best direct/long ball teams of the past tended to have a striker who was dominant in the air. Newcastle do not currently have one which does limit their threat from flick ons.

Newcastle break from defending a long throw. Wissa carries it 60 yards but with Murphy and Fernadez-Pardo better placed, he tries to shoot from 25 yards and plinks it straight at Trafford, provoking an inevitable ‘Woooooooo’.

From the resulting long throw Elvedi is found at the back post, unmarked and attempts to volley it towards goal, missing the ball entirely. It was so wild that even the Leeds staff laugh at how inept it was.

Leeds have a corner when they use one of their signature moves, Bogle cutting in from the right across the back four to take a ball over the top. He controls it but cannot force it past Thiaw.

Hornicek claws out the corner to Bogle 18 yards out. He puts his laces through a volley that Hornicek parries up high and punches away when he has a second go.

Newcastle chip it long again, this time down the right. Gudmundsson holds off Murphy and Leeds will have the relief of a goal-kick.

Leeds are finding it hard now to play through Newcastle’s high press and the intensity with which they are hounding keeper and defenders.

Newcastle keep looking to use their pace with balls over the top for Wissa, Murphy and Fernandez-Pardo. Wissa closes Trafford down quickly again. He needs to release it with more urgency.

Gonzalez hs not recovered from being struck on the head by the ball and is being replaced by Steur as a concussion sub.

Justin heads over his own bar when Newcastle chip a long pass down the inside right. Wissa beats Muharemovic and tries to find Fernandez-Pardo but Justin got there first. Newcastle go short from the corner and Leeds force them back into their own half.

Terrific save from Hornicek down low to his right. Tanaka’s cross from the left found Justin creeping round the back on the right and heading across goal from the back post. Bogle swivelled and tried a sidewinder flick that was arrowing towards the bottom left corner until the keeper swooped to turn it away with his right hand.

Wissa is ticking, feeling he is getting nothing from the referee when challenging for the ball, the latest incident involving a collision with Justin which was 50-50.

Leeds have been the slicker of the two sides, their passing and movement causing the full-backs problems. Okafor dribbles down the left and centres. Stach lays it back to Ampadu who hammers a half-volley from 18 yards that poleaxes Calvert-Lewin who was in an offside position.

Newcastle fans sing ‘There’s only one Kevin Keegan’ as the visitors’ defence sweeps the ball around. When they knock the ball up the inisde-right channel Wissa is penalised for swinging his arm and catching Muharemovic in the mooey.

Wissa presses Trafford high and the goalkeeper is a bit too casual but gets away with it. His clearance bounces off the attacker’s shin and loops out to the right. Leeds shift it quickly out to the left with Gudmundsson and Okafor bombing forward. A vicious cross from the left-back hits a Newcastle leg, loops up and smaxks Gonzales flush in the face, knocking him off his feet. The ref stops play.

Two bad moments for Newcastle early on. Lewis Hall caught out by a simple run and pass behind him and then, from the resulting corner Mathias Fernandez-Pardo looked very fortunate, in my opinion, to avoid conceding a penalty for handball.

He got the benefit of the doubt presumably because the ball bounced up onto his hand as he tried to bring it under control and he did not intend to control it with his hand or knock it away. The handball law confuses me but there is a higher threshold now.

Stach tackles Wissa in the centre-circle. Wissa is playing behind Fernandez-Pardo. Ampadu receives a long pass over the top, coming back from an offside position in the nick of time.

Fernandez-Pardo’s outstretched left arm is struck in the penalty area with the ball after they win the header but the ref waves play on and stops the game for a foul on the new striker.

It’s never a problem to come to Elland Road and the singing of Marching On Together before kick-off makes this one of the top three atmospheres in the country, easily. There are problems with VAR, though, and the whole stadium has just seen the ball strike Matias Fernanzes-Pardo’s hand in the area. The reason it is a problem is because we have become conditioned to thinking every time a ball touches someone on the arm in the area, a penalty should be awarded. It is preposterous that faceless beaks have distorted the game so much.

Leeds kick off, attacking the South Stand, from left to right, as they always prefer to do. Justin and Bogle combine on the right and Bogle bends a pass inside HAll to Stach who chooses to cross rather than shoot. It hits Botman and goes out for a corner.

Leeds are in their home kit of white with yellow and blue pinstripe hoops, Newcastle in their navy away kit.

Anthony [Elanga] is injured. Unfortunately we have to investigate further how long he will be out but obviously we miss him. We wish him to come back as quickly as possible. It could be [a long-term injury] but he will get another MRI next week and then we’ll see.

Lewis Hall is the perfect player profile for how we play. he is a young lad still and we are very excited [that he has signed a new contract].

The start was not easy. We didn’t have lots of time to prepare for pre-season and that’s one reason we are happy and satisfied with the start. But there is potential and we will work hard on the margins we want to improve.

There will be a lot of excitement surrounding Mathias Fernandez-Pardo’s first start for Newcastle United following his deadline day move from Lille but also keep an eye on Jacob Murphy on the right wing.

Fernandez-Pardo starts with a clean slate at Newcastle, Murphy has a lot of baggage and he has been a popular online target for criticism over the last year or so.

Indeed, some sections of the fanbase were stunned Newcastle rejected a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest on deadline day for a player who has entered the final 12 months of his contract.

Murphy has his limitations, sure and he can be infuriating sometimes when he gives the ball away cheaply, but there is a reason Matthias Jaissle was adamant he could not be sold.

Part of that is due to the fact he does not have another specialist right winger behind Anthony Elanga who misses the Leeds game through injury.

But Murphy is also valued for his experience and his training ground presence. He has been at the club a long time, working under Rafa Benítez, Steve Bruce and Eddie Howe and is a boyhood Newcastle fan.

Jaissle was not willing to lose that from his dressing room. Ultimately, though, Murphy has to perform on the pitch to justify the faith shown in him.

There are not many other options to fill that position while Elanga is missing. Harvey Barnes does not like playing on the right, Amar Dedic is a full back and so is Tino Livramento.

This is an opportunity for Murphy to silence his detractors and prove the faith Jaissle has put in him is not misplaced. At the age of 31, he knows he is not the most popular or appreciated player at the club but he has never shirked or complained about that.

He formed a potent partnership with Alexander Isak when he was leading the line for Newcastle. Can he do the same with the new boy Fernandez-Pardo?

Mind you I remember his visit to Elland Road in 1982-83. Not for the faint hearted. In fact it was a disgrace when he was hit by a coin. And yet he was always gracious about Leeds and particularly fond of Don Revie. He was one of very few football people without a strong Leeds United connection who went to his funeral in 1989.

Apparently he was injured in training, the nature of the injury is unspecified.

Newcastle have made a very good start particularly in their transitional moments on the counter-attack. We have to be switched on today to get the next points.

After many years of suffering our supporters deserve it [high expectations]. It’s good but we are far away from not being humble. Our feet are on the ground. We know the second year is always difficult. We have made a good start and it is always important to ride the momentum as long as possible.

Eddie Howe has left a legacy and the culture he created is still around. Matthias has to work with it. They are unbeaten. they are very dangerous with many pacy players up front. It’s important not to lose the ball too easily and always be switched on against Newcastle.

Leeds United Trafford; Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic; Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson; Stach, Okafor; Calvert-Lewin. Substitutes Zetterer, Bard, Bijol, Longstaff, Aaronson, Wilson, James, Bahoya, Nmecha.

Newcastle United (4-2-3-1) Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; González, L Miley; Murphy, Fernandez-Pardo, Barnes; Wissa. Substitutes Pope, Livramento, Schär, Bamba, Steur, Touré, Willock, Ramsey, M Miley.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of Leeds United vs Newcastle United, the last Premier League match of the fourth round of fixtures for the 2026-27 season. Both clubs have made unbeaten starts with one win and two draws each and a win today for wither would send them up to fourth. The two sides met at Elland Road in the third match of last season which ended in a 0-0 draw but the return fixture at St James’ Park was one of the games of the season, a ding-dong match that Leeds led 0-1, 1-2 and 2-3, the latter until the 91st minute and yet still lost 4-3.

The architect of that victory for Newcastle was the Leeds’ fans’ incubus, a player commonly known around Elland Road as ‘Harvey F------- Barnes’. His two goals that night were his sixth and seventh against Leeds in eight matches for Leicester and the Toon. Back in the last century and at the turn of this one, Alan Shearer scored 21 league goals in 23 games against Leeds for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle, it can feel like one bogeyman passing the baton to another.

Newcastle’s sound form with their new model team this season has been based on searing pace and their ability on the counter whether with runners, in the case of Anthony Elanga, or with long diagonals against Tottenham that ripped a hole in the left side of their defence. Leeds rallied from being overrun by Brentford at half-time in their last home game to switch from three at the back to four and wrest back the initiative and while they reverted for the Brighton draw, in both games it was the introduction of Ao Tanaka in midfield that gave them control.

It is genuinely hard to decide whether the 6-3 defeat by Chelsea in the Carabao Cup from being 2-0 up at Stamford Bridge is significant to Leeds league form. One simplistic way of looking at it would be to say Leeds reserves were better than Chelsea’s reserves in the first half and Chelsea’s first-team were better than Leeds reserves and their shaky, debutant keeper in the second. But any similar defensive frailties tonight and there will be jitters over the next week before the international break. Newcastle, by contrast, toiled in their 1-0 victory over Millwall but the result glosses over a lack of incision for long spells of it.

Joe Rodon is out for Leeds for at least another month while Newcastle have changed to withholding information about their treatment room under Matthias Jaissle who says that it should be ‘confidential’. We do know that Joelinton, William Osula and Dan Burn are likely to still be out given the nature of their injuries but Amar Dedic, who came off at half-time at the New Den with a thigh or hamstring problem, may be back.

#1499. Svilar’s condition improves ahead of Parma-Roma

Mile Svilar suddenly stopped playing, leaving the entire Roma fanbase breathless.

It was early October, and his little toe gave way: a stress fracture, a bothersome injury that needed to be overcome as quickly as possible.

The Giallorossi goalkeeper was sidelined for nine games, with Gollini and Vasquez trying to replace him. It’s impossible not to miss him, given that the former Benfica player, in terms of performance, is the best goalkeeper in Serie A.

Svilar is a sure thing for Gian Piero Gasperini’s Roma, almost always among the best on the pitch. Precise, cool, quick, capable of turning the impossible into the possible, but also of shrinking the net to the point where opposing attackers begin to suspect they’ve chosen the wrong profession.

As Corriere dello Sport reports, the 1999-born player’s little finger has stopped hurting. There’s no longer any discomfort. Yesterday, Svilar returned to defend the Trigoria goalposts, darting from post to post without fear.

The worst is now behind him. His foot is fine, his head and reflexes are there: he’ll be back in the starting lineup against Parma. This news reassures Gasperini, the team, and especially the Roma fans.

#1497. PSV raise Van Bommel’s pricetag to 50 million

Roma is searching for strikers ahead of the January transfer window to improve Gian Piero Gasperini’s squad.

The coach is looking for a pacey winger who can add some of the qualities lacking in the attack. In addition to Endrick and Gittens, the Giallorossi are also pursuing Ruben Van Bommel.

The 192cm-tall, 2004-born player would inevitably bring the physicality that’s lacking in the Roma attack. However, the Dutch winger is performing well, boosting PSV’s valuation.

PSV is putting up a wall for Ruben Van Bommel. As reported by Tuttosport, the Dutch club has announced that the 2004-born player’s value is the same as Saibari, whom they sold to Bayern Munich: approximately €50 million.

#1496. Man Utd manager debuts ranked since Sir Alex Ferguson: Pochettino next

After replacing Michael Carrick in the dugout, Mauricio Pochettino starts his reign as Manchester United head coach with a game against Liverpool at Anfield.

Pochettino is set to become the 12th manager to take charge of a United game since Sir Alex Ferguson retired at the end of the 2012/13 season.

We’ve taken a look at how his predecessors fared in their first competitive game in charge of United, ranking them from worst to best.

Following the appointment of Van Gaal and six wins out of six in pre-season, United fans were full of optimism ahead of the 2014/15 campaign.

But the mood changed just 28 minutes into the season when Ki Sung-yueng gave Swansea City the lead at Old Trafford.

Wayne Rooney acrobatically levelled for United early in the second half, before Gylfi Sigurdsson fired home to give the visitors all three points.

“When you have preparation, win everything, then lose your first match, it cannot be worse,” Van Gaal said. “We have built up a lot of confidence. It will be smashed because of this.”

It was also the first time United had lost at Old Trafford on the opening day of the season since a 3-2 defeat against Ipswich Town in 1972.

Eight years after Van Gaal’s United debut, Ten Hag followed in the footsteps of his compatriot by losing 2-1 at home in his first game in charge.

United began the 2022/23 season by welcoming Brighton to Old Trafford and Ten Hag’s team news raised a few eyebrows, with Christian Eriksen debuting in the false nine role and Cristiano Ronaldo named on the bench.

They were outplayed by the Seagulls in the opening period and Pascal Gross’ first-half double saw them trailing 2-0 at the interval.

Ronaldo was brought on in the second half and Alexis Mac Allister’s own goal halved the deficit, but United were unable to find an equaliser.

Despite wanting to stay at Sporting CP until the end of the 2024/25 season, Amorim ultimately agreed to take over at United in November 2024.

His first game was against Ipswich Town at Portman Road and it got off to a perfect start, with Marcus Rashford scoring inside the opening two minutes.

But the hosts were the better side for the rest of the first half, and Omari Hutchinson scored the equaliser just before the break.

United dominated possession in the second half but didn’t create many chances, and they needed a brilliant save from Andre Onana to prevent Ipswich from taking all three points.

One of five former United players on this list, Fletcher was placed in caretaker charge following the decision to sack Amorim in January 2026.

His first game saw United face Burnley at Turf Moor, and he immediately moved away from the Portuguese coach’s 3-4-3 set-up in favour of a back four.

But the change in formation didn’t have an immediate impact, and they fell behind in the 13th minute when Ayden Heaven turned into his own net from a Bashir Humphreys cross.

Benjamin Sesko netted a brace in a 10-minute spell at the start of the second half, before the hosts drew level with a brilliant strike from Jaidon Anthony.

Shea Lacey hit the crossbar in the final stages as United dominated proceedings, but they were unable to find a winner.

Rangnick agreed a six-month deal to become United’s interim manager in November 2021, but work permit issues delayed his arrival.

The German, who is renowned for a high-pressing style, was finally in the dugout for Crystal Palace’s trip to Old Trafford at the start of the following month.

His influence was clear in a breathless opening 30 minutes as United pressed from the front and played at a noticeably quicker tempo.

Their performance petered off after that strong start, but a 77th-minute strike from Fred gave United a fully deserved 1-0 victory.

“With just the one training session, I was really impressed,” Rangnick said after the game. “We did much better than expected.”

The first competitive game in the post-Ferguson era saw Moyes lead United out at Wembley to face Wigan in the 2013 Community Shield.

United were strong favourites against a side that had just been relegated from the Premier League, and Robin van Persie headed home the opening goal inside the opening six minutes.

Van Persie’s deflected strike doubled United’s lead on the hour mark, and that signalled a comfortable end to proceedings.

The celebrations were mooted, and it proved to be both the first and last piece of silverware that Moyes lifted at United.

Van Nistelrooy joined Ten Hag’s coaching staff in the summer of 2024 and took over as interim manager a few weeks later.

He delivered goals throughout his playing career at Old Trafford, and his first game in the dugout was a seven-goal thriller against Leicester City in the Carabao Cup.

Casemiro and Bruno Fernandes both netted braces in the last-16 tie, while Alejandro Garnacho also got on the scoresheet in a 5-2 home win.

Despite still being part of United’s first-team squad, Giggs was named interim manager after Moyes was sacked in April 2014.

His first match in the dugout saw United face Norwich City at Old Trafford, and he was met with a rapturous reception as he emerged from the tunnel.

But United started slowly, and the first half looked set to finish goalless until Danny Welbeck was felled in the area and Wayne Rooney converted a 43rd-minute penalty.

Rooney doubled their lead at the start of a much improved second half before Juan Mata came off the bench to score a brace of his own, giving United a comfortable 4-0 victory.

One of two Carrick entries on this list, the former United midfielder was initially placed in temporary charge after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was sacked in November 2021.

He began his first spell as interim manager with an away game against Villarreal in the Champions League group stage, and David De Gea kept United in the game with two great saves either side of halftime.

Carrick’s substitutions helped change the flow of the game, and Cristiano Ronaldo broke the deadlock in the 78th minute before Jadon Sancho made it 2-0 in injury time.

The win against the Yellow Submarine saw United secure top spot in their Champions League group with a game to spare.

Despite winning the FA Cup final in 2016, Van Gaal was sacked by United and Mourinho was in charge when they returned to Wembley for the Community Shield.

Mourinho went into the game having lost his three previous Community Shields and United had to face the then-reigning Premier League champions Leicester City.

United started brightly in the traditional curtain-raiser, and Jesse Lingard added to his FA Cup final-winning goal with a stunning solo effort.

Jamie Vardy equalised at the start of the second half before Zlatan Ibrahimovic marked his competitive United debut by heading home the winner in the 83rd minute.

Mourinho’s third-season syndrome kicked in once again, and Solskjaer replaced him on an initial interim basis in December 2018.

His first game in the dugout saw him return to the Cardiff City Stadium, having had a 30-game spell in charge of the Welsh side in 2014.

Marcus Rashford fired United in front with a brilliant free-kick in the third minute, while goals from Ander Herrera and Anthony Martial gave the visitors a 3-1 lead at half-time.

A second-half brace from Jesse Lingard made it a comprehensive win as United scored five goals in a Premier League game for the first time since Ferguson retired.

Carrick and Solskjaer were both interviewed by United in January 2026, with the former ultimately being handed the job until the end of the season.

But he began his second spell in the Old Trafford dugout with a daunting first assignment: a Manchester derby.

The manager was still able to oversee an immediate improvement, and second-half goals from Bryan Mbeumo and Patrick Dorgu gave United a 2-0 win over Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City.

It was a thoroughly deserved victory for United, who also hit the woodwork twice and had three goals ruled out for offside.

“It’s an easy thing to say but I couldn’t ask for any more from the boys,” Carrick said after the game. “They gave everything.

“We only had three days to prepare and they took everything on board, tactically, and to be able to deal with it emotionally was exactly as we hoped for.”

#1495. Malen sponsors Gittens’ potential move to Roma

Roma continues to monitor several prospects to strengthen Gian Piero Gasperini’s attack.

Among the first names on the list is Chelsea’s Jamie Gittens: born in 2004, he made his mark with 17 goals and 12 assists between the ages of 18 and 21 at Borussia Dortmund, before falling through the cracks due to injuries and lackluster performances.

According to Corriere dello Sport, Roma is ready to gamble on his relaunch: a loan deal with an option to buy. Napoli are also interested in the Englishman, but Roma has an additional asset: Donyell Malen.

The Dutch striker is very familiar with Gittens, having played alongside him for two and a half years at Borussia Dortmund.

Gittens is going through a tough time at Chelsea, despite the English club’s €56 million investment about a year and a half ago. The 2004-born player has only played 55 minutes this season, which is why he could start elsewhere, far from London.

Roma have been considering him since last season, and Malen, his former teammate, had already spoken highly of the English winger. This detail could accelerate a deal that has been delayed for a few months.

#1494. Ranking all 27 signings Tottenham made under Mauricio Pochettino

Mauricio Pochettino may have operated with one hand tied behind his back at times when it comes to signing players for Tottenham – but how did the transfers he was able to complete fare?

Spurs famously failed to sign a single player in the summer of 2018 and followed that with a similarly fruitless January, but ironically it was when Pochettino did get money to spend in 2019 that things started to go wrong.

He’ll be hoping his new recruitment team at Manchester United can give him a good helping hand in his new job, but it might take a while before United overtake Spurs as the club people most easily associate Pochettino with.

Pochettino signed 27 players in his five years in charge of Tottenham, and we’ve ranked each of those signings, starting off with the stinkers.

Tottenham actually beat Arsenal to the €12million signing of N’Jie from Lyon, all for the sake of eight substitute appearances in the Premier League before he was sent back to Ligue 1.

Cameroon boss Hugo Broos offered an insight into why the winger’s move to north London possibly didn’t work out when accusing him of not working hard enough.

“He must change his attitude and put in the work required if he is to turn the qualities he possesses into success at the top level,” Broos said.

“Even Ronaldo or Messi are always working hard; him thinking that he’s the best doesn’t work, it doesn’t work in Marseille either.”

Clinton N'Jie's shot against Atlético Madrid in all its glory.

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) May 16, 2018

“I have not wasted my time in England.” As far as an evaluation of your time at a club goes, Stambouli’s doesn’t sound too promising.

Stambouli arrived at White Hart Lane with a burgeoning reputation after helping Montpellier win Ligue 1 and often captaining the side at the age of 23.

But the midfielder failed to make an impression at Spurs and was sold after just one season, somehow at a profit, to PSG, where he also lasted a solitary campaign.

We have an element of sympathy for Janssen. Being a backup striker for a team who don’t really play to your strengths seems like a hard gig. But it was made even harder in this instance by the fact Janssen was just a bit… erm… crap.

To be fair to him, he deserved plenty of credit for somehow wrangling the No.9 shirt for the second half of the 2018-19 season despite not appearing for the side since August 2017.

In 2019 he was sold to Monterrey in Mexico for a reported £6.3million, £10.7million less than Spurs had paid for him three years earlier.

This is a bit awkward because Fazio was generally quite good after leaving Tottenham – Gabriel Batistuta even named his fellow Argentine among some of the best defenders in the world in 2017.

But getting sent off twice within the first four months of his Spurs career set a tone which never really changed.

Burnt by the signing of a young, unproven winger from Ligue 1, Spurs decided to replace Clinton N’Jie with Nkoudou, a young, unproven winger from Ligue 1.

He cost them £11million and was sold three years later for £4.6million after a grand total of 10 Premier League appearances.

But we did like his self-effacing follow-up to assisting Harry Winks’ late winner against Fulham in a rare Premier League appearance.

— GK NKoudou ⚡️ (@gknkoudou) January 20, 2019

Given it was Daniel Levy who decided Spurs should sign Clarke from Leeds, there’s an argument to say he shouldn’t even be on this list.

Either way, he cost £10million, was not wanted by Pochettino – at least initially – and never played a single minute of league football for Spurs.

Loans at Leeds, QPR and Stoke did not work out, but he showed signs of improvement while out at Sunderland in 2021-22 and helped them back into the second tier. Still, £10million.

READ MORE: Man Utd reunion? An XI of Pochettino signings sealed by Paul Mitchell

Aurier was quite an expensive signing from PSG and failed to establish himself ahead of Kieran Trippier at right-back.

Then Trippier was sold and was very, very sorely missed.

Tottenham’s record signing at the time, Ndombele provided us with some wonderful moments of skill. But for £60million, we really expected more than a few moments.

Again, good moments. And a spell of genuinely influential form under Jose Mourinho in 2020.

But nowhere near enough to justify the £42million Spurs forked out in combined loan and transfer fees.

In 2015, Yedlin arrived at Tottenham as a very fast, young player who lacked the technical and tactical qualities to really shine at the highest level of the game.

In 2016, Yedlin left Tottenham as a very fast, young player who lacked the technical and tactical qualities to really shine at the highest level of the game.

He only ever made one appearance, but Spurs sold him at a profit to Newcastle, where he made over 100 appearances before going to Galatasaray. That profit alone has shifted him a few places up this ranking.

Lopez never actually played for Tottenham, but he did give our good friend Matt Stead at Football365 the opportunity to regularly upset people by writing that the goalkeeper was an Irishman called Paul O’Pez.

Plus, he was only ever signed on loan to be third-choice goalkeeper so, unlike some of the others, at least he didn’t do anything wrong.

Michel Vorm was fine and these kind of signings are boringly necessary. Sorry.

We also really enjoyed his explanation for signing a new deal at the club in the summer of 2018: “I didn’t have other options.”

He left in 2019 and failed to find another club that summer. But after an injury to Hugo Lloris a few months later, he returned to Spurs on a short-term deal to provide cover. He made one more appearance before retiring in 2020.

Another one who goes in the early promise, a few good games, then not much else category. The saving grace with Foyth is the £5million or so profit they made on him.

We were absolutely convinced Sanchez had all the attributes to succeed at Spurs – and potentially to become one of the best centre-backs in the league – when he signed from Ajax in 2017. And he played more than 200 games for Spurs in the end.

But we can’t help but feel slightly disappointed at how it all turned out for him. He didn’t quite reach his potential. A shame.

Pochettino really liked Gazzaniga, who hails from the same town in Argentina as the former Spurs boss and also played under him at Southampton.

“It was a bit crazy,” Gazzaniga told ESPN in 2018. “Mauricio had a relationship with my granddad and especially my dad, because they played against each other with Instituto and Newell’s Old Boys, and my uncle went to school with him when they were children. It was a big coincidence.”

Coincidence is perhaps not the word we’d choose.

Anyway, Gazzaniga was more than serviceable when he turned out for Spurs, even if he never established himself as a genuine contender to Hugo Lloris.

Signed for £4.3million from Cologne in 2015, Wimmer was a reliable backup in his two seasons at Spurs and impressed when thrust into the team following an injury to Jan Vertonghen early in 2016.

He helped Spurs win six and draw two of a nine-game run in the team, earning himself a new five-year deal in the process, but he was back to being a back-up once Vertonghen returned and only made five Premier League appearances in 2016-17.

Somehow, however, Spurs sold him to Stoke for £18million. Halfway through the season he was on an individual fitness regime and not being considered for the first team even as Stoke hurtled towards relegation.

Starting a petition to re-sign Kevin Wimmer for the sole purpose of keeping Son happy, if anyone is interested. https://t.co/z9L7lKCyiB

— James Harris (@JamesCHarris97) February 3, 2019

It took a while but, at the back end of the 2021-22 season, Ryan Sessegnon finally started to show that he could be a good long-term option for Spurs.

Did he actually become the long-term option for Spurs? No. He didn’t justify his £25million fee, but has at least established himself elsewhere in the Premier League back at Fulham.

Watching Llorente for Spurs was at times pretty uncomfortable.

We’ve already said with regards to Janssen that playing as a backup striker and being expected to score goals when thrown into a team which hardly plays to your strengths, with little match practice, must be pretty difficult.

Llorente definitely made it look pretty difficult. But he also scored a few goals – as he did throughout his career for Europe’s biggest teams – and his hold-up play was excellent.

And his contributions to Spurs’ run to the Champions League in 2019 mean that, despite being released at the end of that season, he’ll always be remembered fondly.

Injuries hampered Wanyama, but the former Southampton man was excellent in his debut season at Spurs after joining for only £11million, helping the north Londoners finish second in the Premier League.

Quite frankly, we would have paid £11million for this goal alone.

One year ago today, Victor Wanyama delivered the ball back into the Liverpool net with real interest. https://t.co/nku4aiyZW6

— Football Ramble (@FootballRamble) February 4, 2019

For a long while it looked like Sissoko would be at the other end of this list, hovering somewhere around Stambouli and Fazio.

After all, for a club which hardly splashes the cash, a £30million outlay on a player who started just eight Premier League games in his debut campaign tends to suggest a bit of a f*ck up.

But, slowly but surely, Pochettino began to iron out the inconsistency and unpredictability and turn Sissoko from a punchline of a right-winger into a combative, all legs-and-lungs central midfielder.

There was plenty of excitement when Spurs parted with £25million to land the forward from PSG, but it took the Brazil international six months to adapt to English football.

After initially underwhelming, Moura shone in his first full season, most notably scoring that incredible second-half hat-trick at Ajax to fire Spurs to the Champions League final.

He was ultimately usurped by Dejan Kulusevski, but we were still tempted to make him No.1 for this reaction alone.

An emotional Lucas Moura hears the commentary from Brazil of his winner for Spurs at Ajax (via @Esp_Interativo) pic.twitter.com/xr2a4sLZez

— Guardian sport (@guardian_sport) May 9, 2019

The absolute definition of a solid club servant. And Spurs only paid £13.5million for him and Vorm combined. Bargain.

Trippier wasn’t able to maintain his 2017-18 form following the World Cup, but perhaps the right-back used up a career’s worth of highs in Russia.

And the fact Spurs were able to sell him to Atletico Madrid for £20million in 2019 tells you he was still pretty decent in 2018-19. Considering he only cost £3.5million, it’s safe to say he goes down as a success.

Another player who seems to attract both over-the-top praise and criticism, Dier was popular with Pochettino and forced himself into the team under all of the managers who’ve followed the Argentine. That’s not a coincidence.

A largely unknown £4million signing from Sporting Lisbon going on to appear over 300 times for Spurs and becoming an established England international generally signifies a very good bit of business.

He stagnated big time during his last couple of years at Spurs, but just think back to those heady days in 2016 when he was playing off Harry Kane, making late runs into the box and finding the net with unerring regularity. Wonderful stuff.

✨🌏✨ A world-class goal from Dele Alli ✨🌏✨#GoalOfTheDay pic.twitter.com/eJHJk5t4sD

— Premier League (@premierleague) September 17, 2021

It’s easy to forget quite how complicated a transfer saga Alderweireld’s signing became for Tottenham, with the defender joining from Atletico Madrid despite Southampton wanting to exercise their option to sign the player on a permanent deal after a successful loan spell.

The £11.4million deal was worth all the headaches, however, as he quickly struck up one of the best defensive partnerships in the league with fellow Belgian and former Ajax team-mate Jan Vertonghen.

Quite possibly the most fun and undoubtedly one of the most brilliant footballers in the Premier League in his prime.

Thank God they didn’t sell him after a difficult first season. We absolutely love him.

#1493. The 9 players with a €1billion release clause: Yamal, Mbappe, Vinicius…

Barcelona and Real Madrid get around Spain’s mandatory release by protecting their top stars with a €1billion release clause that would be beyond even Saudi Pro League clubs.

Some of the best players in the world – and others very much not so – have gigantic clauses in their contracts.

Here are the nine players who reportedly have a €1billion release clause in their contracts.

The midfielder set Barcelona’s precedent with a record €1billion when he signed his a contract extension in October 2021.

After putting his injury woes behind him, Pedri got back to his best as a key cog in 2024-25’s treble chase under Hansi Flick.

Arguably the best midfielder in world football right now, in January 2025 Barcelona tied down his future to 2030. His release clause hasn’t been touched.

Barcelona’s homegrown starlet followed Pedri’s lead and signed a deal running to 2030 – with a new €1billion release clause.

Unlike Pedri, he isn’t a regular starter this season but he’s evidently seen as a big part of the club’s future.

Barcelona signed their prized asset to the maximum three years for a 16-year-old in 2023. Even back then they recognised his potential and made sure he wouldn’t be going anywhere with a €1billion release clause.

He’s now under contract until 2031 and firmly established as one of the best players in the world.

Kounde attracts links with Premier League clubs fairly often, but Barcelona are in a strong negotiating position. He remains contracted in Catalonia until 2030 and included the increasingly commonplace €1billion release clause when they signed him from Sevilla in 2022.

The Brazilian signed a new contract at the Bernabeu in 2022 with a €1billion clause, which remains in place after his latest renewal earlier this year.

There have been times when people have wondered if he’d move on, and if it might actually be beneficial for all concerned, but he remains rooted in Madrid for the foreseeable.

A rare €100million investment that looks worth it, Madrid included the largely symbolic release clause in the England international’s contract when he was signed from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2023.

Madrid believed they were signing one of the top prospects in European football when they signed Camavinga as a teenager from Rennes back in 2021.

His versatility has certainly proven useful, while his early promise earned him a bumper payrise in a bumper new contract in 2023 with a new release clause that rose to €1billion.

There are some question marks over how he’s developed and whether he’ll truly be the future of the Madrid midfield, but he’s established himself pretty well.

Rodrygo signed his last contract extension back in 2023, a five-year deal running through to 2028.

There have been times of speculation over him leaving, but he remains committed to Los Blancos and can’t exactly go anywhere while coming back from a serious injury.

#1492. Hey, Jude! England's star man Bellingham gets celebratory kiss from girlfriend Ashlyn Castro in a rare public appearance together after he led the Three Lions to beating world champions Spain

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:53 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 04:20 EST, 16 November 2026

Jude Bellingham sealed England's stunning 3-2 victory over world champions Spain with a kiss from girlfriend Ashlyn Castro as the couple made a rare public appearance together on Sunday.

England, who romped to a 3-0 lead with a superb display before the hour mark, were forced to weather a late onslaught from the Spanish after Elliot Anderson was shown a red card in the 63rd minute of the Nations League clash.

Although Mikel Oyarzabal and Nico Williams managed to claw two back for this year's World Cup winners, England held on with a backs-to-the-wall effort in the closing stages, courtesy of a few fine saves from Leeds goalkeeper James Trafford.

After England's victory, which called an end to Spain's historic 43-game unbeaten run, Bellingham was spotted celebrating with his model girlfriend Ashlyn inside the stadium.

Wearing a beaming smile, he went over to embrace both the 28-year-old American and his father Mark as the family soaked up the celebrations in the stands.

The Real Madrid superstar has largely kept his relationship with Ashlyn private since the pair were first linked in early 2025.

Jude Bellingham and his girlfriend Ashlyn Castro celebrate England's superb win over Spain

The Real Madrid star then caught up with his dad Mark on a special night for the Bellinghams

Ashlyn is a model and social media influencer from California (@instagram/ashlyncastro)

Ashlyn is a model and social media influencer from California who boasts over one million followers on Instagram, sharing fashion and beauty content online.

Spanish media waxed lyrical about Bellingham's display on the night, claiming he was 'determined to make a statement' at the stadium of Real Madrid's rivals Atletico.

Newspaper AS wrote: 'If anyone felt the match was crucial, it was Jude Bellingham. He stepped onto the Metropolitano pitch determined to make a statement, to impose his usual footballing and physical prowess.

'He exudes football in every movement, and his rise to the top is unstoppable.'

It was a proud international break for the Bellinghams before a ball was kicked in Madrid, with Jude's 21-year-old younger brother Jobe also earning his first England call-up last week.

Jude and Jobe would have become the first brothers to play for England since Gary and Phil Neville 17 years ago, but the younger sibling stayed on Thomas Tuchel's bench as an unused substitute.

England, who topped Group C on goal difference over Spain, will now not play until the Nations League quarter-finals kick off next spring.

The final, should Tuchel's Three Lions make it that far, are scheduled for the summer.

#1491. Superb XI of players out of contract in 2027: Decision time for these stars…

When a player enters the last year of their contract, it leaves their club with a big question: cash in while you can?

The risk of losing a top player for free can strike fear into even the biggest clubs. Thus, once a player’s contract ticks over into its last year, they have to act fast to decide if they’ll be offering a renewal or selling before it’s too late.

There are some high-profile players in that kind of predicament this year and it could lead to some blockbuster moves in 2027.

We’ve picked out an XI of players in the final year of their contracts, arranged conveniently in a 4-2-3-1 formation.

The best goalkeeper in the world? Those of a Real Madrid persuasion would certainly argue so.

Courtois is now 34 and Madrid don’t really do long-term deals for players of his age. But he remains their regular starter and has been named in La Liga’s team of the season for the past two years running, despite his club winning nothing of note in either of them.

We’re pretty sure that as long as he’s at his peak, Courtois will be a Madrid player.

A newly crowned World Cup winner, even though he only played six minutes of football beyond the group stage, Llorente is into the last year of his contract with Atletico Madrid, who he joined from cross-city rivals Real in 2019.

Very much a part of the furniture at the Metropolitano now, the midfielder-turned-right-back emphasised in March: “I want to retire at Atletico. I want to stay longer at the club and hope to reach an agreement for a renewal.”

Could it soon be time for another modern-day Liverpool legend to leave the club?

After Andy Robertson and Mohamed Salah this year, Van Dijk’s long-term future will surely come into question over the next few months.

Now 35, Van Dijk is past his prime but remains a key player for Liverpool. You can picture him retiring there, but some might have thought that about Robertson and Salah.

If it wasn’t for injury issues, Martinez’s future at Manchester United might be secure by now.

But those physical problems will have to be factored in for any decision about the 28-year-old’s future.

And he hasn’t exactly helped himself with comments against the club and some poor performances of his own. Might be best for everyone if he moves on.

Captain of RB Leipzig, Raum has spent his whole career in Germany but it could be time to broaden his horizons.

Now 28, Raum has been linked with a few Premier League clubs over the past couple of transfer windows.

There was a time when Calhanoglu was a classy attacking midfielder with an eye for a spectacular free kick.

In open play, he operates deeper these days. He is in his thirties now, after all. But he remains a key player for Inter and scored three goals in his first four league games this season.

This is now Ayari’s third season as a first-team regular with Brighton and he might be coming into form just at the right time – either for a contract extension or a big move. Classic of the genre.

Ayari has three goals from his first nine games in the Premier League this season and looks well on course for the best campaign of his career.

“I’m at Brighton and I’m happy where I am,” he’s insisted. “Things are going well for me right now. Then we’ll see what’s to come.”

READ: Ranking the 10 best midfielders in world football: Rodri, Rice, Vitinha…

Real Madrid acted quickly to renew another winger whose deal was due to be up in 2027, Vinicius Junior.

Brahim is still waiting for more clarity on his own future, though. He’s only started once in La Liga this season.

Fernandes committed his future to Manchester United last summer in the face of interest from Saudi Arabia and they were glad of it as he went on to break the record for the most assists in a Premier League season.

The 32-year-old still has huge ambitions for what he wants to achieve with United, so you’d suspect he still has unfinished business at Old Trafford.

But will their union last forever? It could be on shaky ground at the moment.

Mitoma used to dazzle in the Premier League with Brighton, before going off the boil a bit.

He’d still be a smart pickup for someone on a free, though, if the Seagulls can’t extend his stay. He’s been out all season with a hamstring injury, mind you, and any potential suitors will have to be wary.

We probably should have put Jean-Philippe Mateta in here, but can’t look past Ronaldo. Come on, you can’t blame us.

He’s retired from international duty with Portugal, but still has a few months of commitment left with Al-Nassr. Will there be any more after that?

Now in his forties, Ronaldo is in the endgame of his career. But someone would surely be tempted to sign him if he was to leave Al-Nassr and put retirement on hold.

#1490. Ranking 7 possible next jobs for Eddie Howe after Man Utd snub

Eddie Howe has been passed over for the Manchester United gig, meaning the ex-Newcastle boss is still on the look for his next job.

Howe has only been out of work for a little under four months but it already feels like many of the opportunities he would have fancied have gone.

Mauricio Pochettino beat him to Old Trafford and so here are his possible options rated by how likely we think they are.

It was Howe’s decision to leave Newcastle but you do wonder if he regrets it slightly.

When he left St James’, there were potential vacancies at England, Manchester United and Spurs and yet all three of those options looked closed off for the time being.

And in terms of the kind of club that would appoint Howe, that second rung below the best of the best does seem the most likely.

Newcastle should be high in that group provided they find a way to make Champions League qualification more consistent and Matthias Jaissle’s struggles may have them calling up Howe to see if he fancies another go.

He probably does not but you can’t rule it out entirely.

Cracks are already starting to appear in the relationship between Oliver Glasner and the Forest hierarchy with him responding to a 2-0 defeat to Brentford at the end of October by saying he had made too many compromises since taking over.

He did not allude to what those compromises were but ignoring them brought an immediate result in the form of a 3-1 victory against Manchester City.

However, Glasner is quite a combustible character and Evangelos Marinakis even more so. It would not be unreasonable to suggest this may be a short partnership.

It would take a lot to sack Glasner with his mega bucks deal but if they do, Howe could be a candidate they go after.

From Howe’s perspective, there are not a huge amount of positives to go off. You would probably get paid a lot of money but the squad is not the best by any stretch of the imagination and you would be signing up for a relegation battle you suspect.

Howe probably thinks he is above that at this stage of his career.

Howe has long been linked with the England gig and he was reportedly in the running before Tuchel got it.

But with the German having survived the World Cup fallout, it feels unlikely that seat would be vacant until at least post Euro 2028 and that is a long time out of the game for someone like Howe.

He may well fancy the job but would probably take one in between.

If you can’t get a Premier League job, why not fill your coffers with a stint in Saudi?

Howe has already shown flexibility when it comes to moral objections to Saudi Arabia and so would presumably have no issue in spending a stint over there from that perspective. He would be joining the likes of Ange Postecoglou, Brendan Rodgers and the best-paid manager in the world, Simone Inzaghi.

The problem is that once you go to Saudi, you never really come back and Howe may swerve it to preserve his top-level career.

QUIZ: Can you name every player Eddie Howe used as Newcastle manager?

When Howe took a managerial sabbatical in 2020, he headed to Madrid to watch how Diego Simeone trained his Atletico squad, suggesting he at least acknowledges there is life outside of the Premier League.

For that reason and given the lack of immediate Premier League options, him taking a job in Europe is not completely out of the question.

In terms of the leagues that would suit him, the Bundesliga feels the second most natural fit behind the Premier League given it also plays high-intensity football and so maybe a team away from Dortmund or Bayern could be where he ends up.

We have seen plenty of English players have success in Europe but a manager doing so is still rare at this stage. You cannot deny though that if Howe does do it, it would make him a better coach.

West Ham have only just appointed Scott Parker but he does feel like the modern Neil Warnock in that he will get you up from the Championship but don’t expect him to keep you there.

This is not the Sullivan and Gold era of West Ham anymore either. A Gold is still in charge as following the death of her father, Vanessa Gold took over as chairwoman, but 43% of the club was bought by Daniel Kretinsky, a Czech billionaire who also co-owns Sparta Prague.

The new owners will have bought West Ham for what it could be rather than the Championship outfit it currently is and turning a lower-half Premier League club into one challenging for Europe is exactly the kind of task Howe did at Newcastle.

For Howe, it will be a question of whether he wants such a project again and he will want assurances that there is money to rejuvenate the squad but it does seem like an ideal job for him should Parker take them up.

The Toffees are sixth in the Premier League but there are still some sections of the Hill Dickinson crowd that are in two minds about David Moyes.

Obviously he has done very well to take them from the threat of relegation and into the top six but the football is not exactly the most thrilling.

Only Leeds have scored fewer of the teams in the top 10 and there is a desire for Everton to play more expansive football, something they have not really done well since Carlo Ancelotti.

Howe’s style is far more high-tempo than Moyes’ and so should be more pleasing for the fans and there are a lot of positives for the former Bournemouth boss to consider.

First of all, the club has the newest stadium in the Premier League, they also have a good squad if a little light, and you could put Everton in that sleeping giant category, even if they have been in that slumber for a long time now.

What he will want is assurances from the ownership. The Friedkin Group have indicated their willingness to sell the club and so Howe may want to wait until a new owner is identified but he could do a lot worse than the Everton job.

#1489. Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town

There is an obligation on all of us, from supporters to pundits and journalists, to remain calm and measured about footballers as young as Max Dowman. But, my word, he does make it difficult. Arsenal’s 16-year-old sensation continues to sparkle whenever he steps on to the field, and he did so again with this superb display against Ipswich Town.

"The hype will only continue to grow!"Max Dowman that is delightful! 👏 pic.twitter.com/UfFY1VSyXn

At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

Max Dowman nets his second of the game! 😍 pic.twitter.com/XRZ9GqZx3x

As Mikel Arteta approaches the point of signing a new contract in north London, one wonders how much the idea of developing Dowman will excite him as he looks to the future. Which manager would not want to coach a player of such natural ability? Which manager would not want to see how good he could be? The same is true of Marli Salmon, the 17-year-old defender who also impressed on Tuesday night.

“A joy to have him,” said Arteta of Dowman. “It’s remarkable. It’s something very natural for him. He can deliver those actions effortlessly, I would say. What we have to do is look after him. He is 16. You don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context.

“Having two teenagers playing for Arsenal at this level is so fulfilling. Because I’ve been there and just to be able to contribute to somebody’s career and dream, to be able to experience a game like tonight, is phenomenal. And yeah, medium and long term, we know that if they continue to develop in the way that they are, we are going to have two tremendous footballers.”

"He was brilliant, he made the difference - we need to look after him" 🌟Mikel Arteta says Arsenal need to "be really cautious" with 16-year-old Max Dowman after he scored twice in Arsenal's 4-2 win over Ipswich 🔴 pic.twitter.com/1msJAEkK8z

Dowman’s two goals, along with strikes by Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino, secured a comfortable victory for Arsenal against Premier League opponents. Ipswich scored a goal of their own, through Anis Mehmeti, but never seemed likely to cause the visitors too much bother. A late strike from former Arsenal player Chuba Akpom was only a consolation. “We found a way to fight back into it,” said Gary O’Neil. “Losing by two goals to them isn’t a dreadful effort.”

Dowman is already developing a trademark goal, of sorts. His first strike for the club, against Everton last season, came after he left an opponent face-down on the turf at the Emirates Stadium. He inflicted the same pain here upon poor Cédric Kipré, who tried to tackle the teenager in the seventh minute but ended up with a mouthful of grass.

It was an image that encapsulated Arsenal’s dominance in the early exchanges, as was the sight of Madueke firing in the second. The chance came after Bruno Guimarães and Merino, majestic in midfield, had monstered Ipswich’s attempts to play out from the back. Merino was dominant throughout, winning tackles with steel and then spinning away opponents with style. “He’s unbelievable,” said Arteta.

Arsenal’s long-term relationship with the League Cup is not a particularly healthy one. For a club of their stature, it is a source of mild embarrassment that they have not won this competition since 1993. They came close last season, reaching the final at Wembley, but were defeated by Manchester City.

Given the depth of Arteta’s squad, Arsenal really should reach the final again. If this is a tournament for the B-team, at least in these early stages, then Arsenal probably have the best B-team in the country. They started this game without any of Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice, Martin Odegaard, and Kai Havertz but were still extraordinarily strong in midfield and attack.

The only pre-match concern was their defence, which has been weakened by a couple of early-season injuries. Arsenal started with Salmon at centre-back and the teenager was in direct combat with the physical, sharp-elbowed threat of Ipswich striker Zian Flemming. He stood up to the challenge with determination and class.

Ipswich had made 10 changes following their victory at Crystal Palace at the weekend, which was an indication of where the Carabao Cup sits in their priorities. They were able to get into Arsenal’s penalty area but never gave the impression they could really hurt the Premier League champions, apart from when Mehmeti converted Jack Clarke’s low cross.

Akpom struck in the 91st minute to encourage O’Neil, but by then the game had been lost. Arsenal’s work, and indeed Dowman’s work, had been done.

"He's 16 years old, and we have to be cautious of that" 💫Mikel Arteta reacts to an incredible performance from Max Dowman as Arsenal put FOUR past Ipswich 🔴Don't miss the Carabao Cup on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/AIcAbMx6ub

On managing the hype that surrounds Dowman, Arteta said: “What we have to do is look after him. He’s 16 years old, you don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context, but in this league, with the demands... We need to make sure that every time we throw him in it’s in the right context with the right preparation.”

Conor Coady shares his thoughts on Arteta’s role in Dowman’s development:

"He'll know how to nurture him!" 🗣️Conor Coady says Mikel Arteta is the perfect manager for Max Dowman 👏 pic.twitter.com/YdgLxfKiOf

Asked about Dowman’s two-goal performance, Arteta said: “A joy to have him, Marli [Salmon] as well. Seventeen years old, to play at that level with the physicality they have to be able to handle that level, it’s remarkable. Max, yeah, it’s inevitable to talk about him when he scores and he creates the moments he has created tonight. It’s normal.”

He added: “He is coping better and better and better, he did the action where he regains the ball and wins it in the first goal, he loses his man... He’s an unbelievable player because of the character that he has and how much he loves to play on the biggest stage and still handles the situation with such naturality.”

Speaking in his post-match press conference, Mikel Arteta said: “Really pleased with a lot of things we did tonight, the way we attacked the game, how dominant, fluid and aggressive we were, right from the beginning to try to influence the result. We scored two very early goals that gave us obviously a great platform for the game.

“Individually some big performances as well. Some debuts tonight which is great to see as well, so we take a lot of positives from tonight.”
